extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (and beginning graduate) students reading a first course/textbook in real analysis; instructors using the book
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal conventions from a first-course real analysis textbook (chapter map, notation standards, and foundational definitions/theorems) intended to direct reading and to fix notation and basic proof conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested reading order and optional sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance about which sections/parts are essential versus optional and prerequisites between chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: In Chapter V Lebesgue measure in one dimension is introduced right away; the Extension Theorem is stated when needed but proved only after basic convergence theorems (proof in Sections 5–6 may be skipped on first reading). Section 7 (Fubini) prepares Chapter VI construction of n-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Section 10 in Chapter V is applied only in Section IX.6. Chapters VII–IX are largely independent; Chapter VII is historically important and motivates Radon–Nikodym but no later chapter is logically dependent on it. Chapter VIII: first four sections are the core; remaining sections are optional if Section IX.6 is omitted. Chapter IX concerns L^p; only Section 6 uses material from Chapter VIII. Chapter XI depends on Chapter X and first five sections of Chapter IX but not on VII–VIII. Appendix B (complex analysis) has explicit prerequisites (Sections 1–7 of Chapter I, Sections 1–8 of Chapter II, Sections 1–3, 5–6, and 11–12 of Chapter III); Appendix B is optional for reading Chapters I–XII but its results are used in problems in Chapters IV, VI, VIII and once in IX.6. Sections 8–10 of Chapter VI are of somewhat less importance and may be omitted if time is short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard notation (table of symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: A canonical list of symbols and their meanings used throughout the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides a standard-notation table giving symbol → meaning mappings (original wording preserved where possible). Examples include: #S or |S| = number of elements in S; ∅ = empty set; {x in E : P} = set of x in E such that P holds; E^c = complement of E; E ⊆ F, F ⊇ E; × = product of sets; (a1,...,an) = ordered n-tuple, {a1,...,an} = unordered n-tuple; f(x) = function value, f : E → F; f◦g = composition; f|E = restriction to E; f(E) and f^{-1}(·) = direct and inverse image; δ_{ij} = Kronecker delta; (n choose k) binomial coefficient; n positive, n negative; Z, Q, R, C; max and min; ∑ and ∏ (sum/product) possibly with a limit operation; countable (finite or in one-one correspondence with Z); [x] = greatest integer; Re z, Im z;  ar{z} = complex conjugate; |z| = absolute value; 1 or I = multiplicative identity; dim V; R^n, C^n; det A, A^tr = transpose, diag(a1,...,an); ∼= = is isomorphic to/is equivalent to. (The table on the page should be used as the canonical symbol reference for this book.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence domain convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition / convention for what counts as a sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sequence is a function whose domain is a certain kind of subset of integers: nonempty, consists of consecutive integers, and contains no largest integer (in practice: all nonnegative integers or all positive integers; sometimes all integers for doubly infinite sequences). Notation: value at n written a_n; sequence sometimes denoted {a_n}_n where outer subscript indicates domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequence definition
rubrics_metrics.description: How subsequences are formed and what their domain is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subsequence of a sequence f is a composition f◦n_k where n_k is a strictly increasing sequence of integers with no largest term (n_k < n_{k+1}). By this definition the domain of a subsequence is always infinite. Example: selecting even terms n_k = 2k gives subsequence {a_{2k}}_k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence (ε–N) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard ε–N definition of convergence for sequences in R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sequence {a_n} in R converges to a in R if for every ε>0 there exists an integer N such that |a_n − a| < ε for all n ≥ N. Notation lim_{n→∞} a_n = a or a_n → a. Default setting for convergence/divergence discussion is R (not the extended reals) unless indicated otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone bounded sequence convergence (Corollary 1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotone bounded sequences converge and the limit equals sup/inf of image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any bounded monotone sequence in R converges. If monotone increasing, limit = sup_n a_n; if monotone decreasing, limit = inf_n a_n. Proof sketch and remark about using this property as an axiom in calculus courses are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean property and density of rationals
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences of the least upper bound property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 1.3 (Archimedean property): for a>0 and any b there exists integer n with n a > b. Corollary 1.4 and 1.5 deduce existence of integers n with n c < n+1 and density of rationals: for x<y there exists rational r with x<r<y. These are stated as elementary standard facts to be used freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended real numbers R* and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce R* = R ∪ {+∞} ∪ {−∞} with ordering and arithmetic conventions (partial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend ordering so −∞ < r < +∞ for all r in R. Define sup and inf for nonempty subsets of R using +∞/−∞ when unbounded. Define arithmetic with infinities but avoid making all operations everywhere defined (to preserve distributive laws). Specific conventions given: for r in R, r·(+∞) = +∞ if r>0, = 0 if r=0, = −∞ if r<0; similarly r·(−∞) = −∞ if r>0, 0 if r=0, +∞ if r<0. Addition/subtraction/division conventions summarized; special cases (like 0 times anything = 0) are emphasized as important for measure theory. Default discussion of convergence is in R unless R* is explicitly invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: lim sup and lim inf definitions and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of lim sup and lim inf via sup/inf of tails and their basic properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define b_n = sup_{k≥n} a_k (monotone decreasing) and lim sup a_n = inf_n b_n (always exists in R*). Similarly lim inf a_n = sup_n inf_{k≥n} a_k. Properties listed: monotonicity under pointwise inequality; lim inf ≤ lim sup; existence of subsequences achieving lim sup and lim inf as subsequential limits; lim sup is supremum of subsequential limits, lim inf is infimum of subsequential limits; if lim sup<+∞ then description via set of a for which a_n>a only finitely often, etc.; sequence converges in R* iff lim inf = lim sup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem (bounded sequence subsequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every bounded sequence in R has a convergent subsequence with limit in R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is provided as a central compactness fact used repeatedly (proof uses lim sup / subsequence construction). The text notes that if all quantities in lim sup formation lie in R then the subsequential limit is in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy criterion (completeness of R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Cauchy sequence in R converges to a limit in R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: sequence is Cauchy if for every ε>0 there exists N such that |a_n − a_m| < ε for all n,m ≥ N. Proof uses boundedness and Bolzano–Weierstrass to extract convergent subsequence, then standard ε–N argument to show full sequence converges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-convention: allowance of fixed multiplicative constants in ε-bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof-writing convention allowing final bound to be M·ε (e.g., '2ε proof') rather than exactly ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text permits taking ε0 = ε/M at start and proving final bound M·ε0 = ε; thus authors will often give bounds like 2ε and denote such a proof a '2ε proof'. This is an explicit stylistic/proof convention for clarity and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform continuity on closed bounded intervals (Heine–Cantor type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous function f on a closed bounded interval [a,b] is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem statement and proof outline: using continuity at each point define δ_x(ε) and then consider δ(ε)=inf_{x∈[a,b]} δ_x(ε); show δ(ε)>0 by contradiction using Bolzano–Weierstrass to extract convergent sequence where δ_xn(ε)→0. This is the canonical argument in the book and should be used when establishing uniform continuity on compact domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme value theorem (boundedness and attainment of extrema)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous function on a closed bounded interval [a,b] is bounded and assumes its maximum and minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses sequences: take sup of f([a,b]) in R* and extract sequence x_n with f(x_n) increasing to sup; apply Bolzano–Weierstrass to obtain convergent subsequence and continuity to conclude sup is attained; analogous for min.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate Value Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b] then f takes on every value between f(a) and f(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by partition/compactness argument: define sets A = {x∈[a,b] : f(x) ≤ α} and B = {x∈[a,b] : f(x) ≥ β} with α=f(a), β=f(b); use supremum/inf and uniform continuity type arguments plus Bolzano–Weierstrass to derive contradiction if intermediate value is not attained. The text remarks a more conceptually clear proof will appear later using connectedness.
